content:
About 2,145 trees expected to be felled

The current project is being undertaken by a joint venture of "China State Construction Hong Kong", "Aiming Construction", and "China State Construction Civil Engineering". According to 2024 Legislative Council documents, the project area contains approximately 2,270 trees, of which about 2,145 are expected to be felled, including 10 "trees of special value" — Aquilaria sinensis (土沉香) — and 2 Ormosia pachycarpa (茸莢紅豆). The authorities plan to replant about 2,140 trees after completion, including Koelreuteria bipinnata (複羽葉欒樹), Magnolia grandiflora (荷花玉蘭) and champaca (黄蘭), among others.

No shade from large trees — residents: heat feels even more intense in hot weather

Reporters recently inspected the area from Lake Court (匡湖居) to Sai Kung Town Centre, and found that trees had been removed along the roads in Pak Wai, Lake Court (匡湖居), Hebe Haven (白沙灣), Pak Kong and Sai Kung Town Centre. The felling was particularly evident in the Pak Kong area; due to site formation works, reporters observed that nearly one-third of the trees on the hillside had been cut down, and at least 15 consecutive trees had been felled along the road near Tai Chung Hau Village (大涌口村). Some village residents said that with the roadside shade diminishing, the heat feels even more oppressive in hot weather.

Site formation works are underway on the Pak Kong hillside, with trees being felled.

One of the felled large trees has been hollowed out, with a bottle of orange juice placed inside.

Unavoidable removal of about 1,900 trees required

In response to inquiries from FactWire (《集誌社》), the Highways Department said that because the relevant works run very close to vegetated slopes on both sides of the road, some trees mainly situated on the slopes had to be removed or transplanted to free up sufficient space for the works. After investigation, the unavoidable removal of about 1,900 trees is still required.

11 of 13 Aquilaria sinensis trees expected to be felled

The authorities said there are 13 Aquilaria sinensis trees within the project area, of which 11 were assessed as unsuitable for transplantation and had to be removed due to their form, structure and growing location; the remaining 2 are being preserved in situ. One Ormosia pachycarpa was also assessed as unsuitable for transplantation and has to be removed; one camphor tree originally earmarked for transplantation was likewise assessed as needing removal. Three Indian rubber trees are being preserved in situ.

The authorities said the project team will plant about 2,000 trees at suitable locations within the Sai Kung district, such as roadside greening belts, to enhance the landscape along the road and the Sai Kung community environment.

Aquilaria sinensis is classified as Vulnerable

Aquilaria sinensis (土沉香) is a native Hong Kong tree species, mainly distributed in Sai Kung, the northeastern New Territories and on Lantau Island. As of 2021, there were about 5,000 mature Aquilaria sinensis trees in Hong Kong. The species is classified as rare and is listed as a protected plant under the Protection of Endangered Species of Animals and Plants Ordinance, and as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. Because its resin can be refined into the valuable fragrance "agarwood", illegal felling gangs from mainland China were once known to come to Hong Kong — particularly to the Sai Kung area — to fell the trees for the black market, where they could fetch over HK$10,000.

As for Ormosia pachycarpa (茸莢紅豆), it is an evergreen tree of the legume family Fabaceae, genus Ormosia, and is classified by the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department as a rare and precious plant. The species was first discovered in Happy Valley in 1850, and is now considered endangered in mainland China.

Pak Wai Village (北圍村) resident Regina bought a village house years ago. A self-confessed "plant lover" (花癡), her decision to buy the house was entirely due to an old tree in front of it, which she likens to a "treasure". After learning of the tree-felling in the surrounding area, she said heatedly: "It's 2,000 trees, not 200!" She believes Sai Kung has long enjoyed the reputation of being "Hong Kong's backyard", and questioned: "Without the 2,000 trees, can Sai Kung still be called Hong Kong's backyard?"

Self-described "plant lover" (花癡) Regina's decision to buy a house in Sai Kung was entirely due to the old tree growing in front of it, which she likens to discovering a "treasure". (Provided by Regina)

She said trees are living things that may take a hundred years to grow; once lost, they cannot easily be restored — including the precious Aquilaria sinensis. Taking Pak Wai Village as an example, she noted that visitors may not remember the village name, but they remember the old tree at the village entrance, which has even become a bus stop landmark. "I can see the mountain precisely because of these trees — try removing them and how would I view the mountain?" She believes the government should not take a one-size-fits-all approach at the expense of nature conservation.

Residents are deeply attached to the old trees

Another Sai Kung resident, Amy, said three generations of her family, including her children, grew up in Sai Kung. "Seeing the trees gone, it's as if all those years of growing up are gone too." Not wearing glasses, she joked that her eyesight has been excellent all these years precisely because she has been surrounded by greenery, gazing out at lush woodlands. "Suddenly they cut them down — even the children will end up needing glasses."

Beyond witnessing the disappearance of the trees, she lamented the changes Sai Kung has undergone over the years. For example, several historic buildings facing the Sai Kung Highway, including the 1946-built China Paint (中華製漆) paint factory — known for its "Chrysanthemum", "Giraffe" and "Toy" brand logos — is to be demolished and redeveloped into residential housing. She also cited as an example an old tree in town that fell during a recent super typhoon, which attracted residents to "check in" on social media, also reflecting residents' deep affection for old trees.

The roadsides have become "patchy and unsightly"

Sai Kung resident Mr Tam said that although he does not know the exact number of trees felled, he has clearly seen the trees along the way diminish. "There used to be lots of trees and it was very pleasant, but now you see it all patchy and broken up — it doesn't feel comfortable." He said when he moved into Sai Kung a year or two ago, large-scale tree felling had not yet begun; he also felt it was a pity that the Aquilaria sinensis were being cut down. He also questioned whether road widening would ease congestion, noting that traffic jams heading into Sai Kung on holidays are expected anyway.

An 84-year-old Sai Kung resident known as "Uncle" (阿伯) has lived in the area for more than 20 years. He said since over a thousand trees were felled, the Sai Kung landscape has become unrecognisable, and questioned: "What's traffic got to do with the trees? Cars don't drive through the trees, do they?"

Friends of the Earth (地球之友) director Wong Cheuk-yuet (王卓粵) said that when consultants assess trees, although it may not be intentional, for the convenience of construction it is easy to fall into the situation of "nitpicking", where if a tree cannot be moved it is simply felled, rather than making efforts to save each one. For instance, ordinary species need to be "virtually flawless" to be retained; even if a tree's condition is not bad, as long as it has a minor defect or slightly less growing space, the report lists adverse factors; and some large trees can deteriorate during transplantation because the cost can easily run into over a million dollars, or because of procedures and difficulty finding a suitable site.

Aquilaria sinensis should in principle be preserved as far as possible

He acknowledged that some parts of Sai Kung are located on slopes, making excavation of root balls and transplantation more difficult, but if conservation is the goal, major crown pruning and reducing the size of root balls should be considered, with the priority being to "preserve the species" and "save its life". With Aquilaria sinensis numbers having fallen significantly, they should in principle be retained wherever possible. He also worries that as the road gains additional lanes and dividing facilities, there will be insufficient space for planting along the route, turning what was once a shady stretch into vast expanses of concrete, which in the long run may affect the experience of waiting for transport and walking.
